ety.text: Old Norse bóndibor. Old English bonda ▲ Old Norse húsbóndicalq. Old English hūsbonda Middle English husbonde English husband Inherited from Middle English husbonde, from Old English hūsbonda, from hūs + bonda. Calque of Old Norse húsbóndi. By surface analysis, house + bond.

senses.d: A man in a marriage or marital relationship, especially in relation to his spouse.
ex: You should start dating so you can find a suitable husband.
The husband and wife are one person in law.

senses.d: A manager of property; one who has the care of another's belongings, owndom, or interests; a steward; an economist.
A prudent or frugal manager.
ex: God knows how little time is left me, and may I be a good husband, to improve the short remnant thereof.

senses.d: The master of a house; the head of a family; a householder.
A tiller of the ground; a husbandman.
ex:
[…] a withered tree, through husbands toyle,
 Is often seene full freshly to have florisht […]
The painfull husband plowing up his ground, Shall finde all fret and rust both pikes and shields

senses.d: The male of a pair of animals.
ex: Husband of the Herd

senses.d: A large cushion with arms meant to support a person in the sitting position.
ex: While reading her book, Sally leaned back against her husband, wishing it were the human kind.

senses.d: A polled tree; a pollard.
To manage or administer carefully and frugally; use to the best advantage; economise.
ex:
And for my meanes, I'll husband them so well,
They shall go farre with little.

senses.d: To conserve.
To till; cultivate; farm; nurture.
ex: Land so trim and rarely husbanded.

senses.d: To provide with a husband.
ex:
Thinke you, I am no ſtronger then my Sex
 Being ſo Father'd, and ſo Husbanded?

senses.d: To engage or act as a husband to; assume the care of or responsibility for; accept as one's own.

Inherited from Latin spōnsus.

pt:marido.gl: husband (male partner in a married couple)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese marido, from Latin marītus (“husband”), from mās (“male, a male”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esposo, from Latin spōnsus.

es:ahorrar.gl: to save (to store for future use)

ety.text: From horro (“free”), from Arabic حُرّ (ḥurr, “free, noble, virtuous”). Compare to Catalan aforrar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese poupar, from Latin palpāre (“to touch softly”). Doublet of the borrowing palpar and apalpar.
From Latin cōnservāre (“to preserve; to conserve”), probably borrowed.

From Middle English huschen (“to hush”) (as past participle husht (“silent; hushed”) and interjection husht (“quiet!”)). Cognate with Low German huschen, hüssen (“to hush; lull”), German huschen (“to shoo; scurry”), Danish hysse (“to hush”), and maybe Albanian hesht.
Unclear; possibly onomatopoeic.

senses.d: To become quiet.
To make quiet.
To appease; to allay; to soothe.
ex: VVilt thou then / Huſh my Cares thus, and ſhelter me vvith Love?
And hush’d my deepest grief of all.

senses.d: A silence, especially after some noise.
ex: It is the hush of night.
And there fell a hush upon the gods when they saw that Māna rested, and there was silence on Pegāna save for the drumming of Skarl.

senses.d: To rush, to gush.
ex: On the fluir, bluid an punch now hush't leyke a stream, […]
[…] water, far down below, roaring and hushing over the rocks, […]

senses.d: To send forth a rush of water over (some ground) so as to clear off the soil and other materials overlying, and thus uncover or separate out, ore.
ex: [He] had promised … that he would have a stop put to the hushing process.

senses.d: Water which has been used to clear the soil off of some (area of) rock or ore.
ex: The great cause of the scarcity of fish in this river is without doubt the "hush" coming down from the lead mines in the upper waters. […]

senses.d: A part of a mine or quarry where ore is to be, or has been, excavated by an artificial flow of water.

chain.g: to let down, allow to hang free

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *callāre, from Latin chalāre, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō). Compare Portuguese calar.
From a- + callar.

es:calmar.gl: to calm, to still (to limit and lessen in motion and disturbance)

Spanish calma Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -āre Old Spanish -ar Spanish -ar Spanish calmar From calma + -ar.
From Latin silentium (“silence”).
Latin -iusnom. Latin -ium Latin silentiumbor. Spanish silencio Borrowed from Latin silentium.
From Dutch husselen or by metathesis from Dutch hutselen (“to shake up”), a frequentative of hutsen (“to stir, to move something (back and forth)”).

senses.d: To push someone roughly; to crowd; to jostle.
To rush or hurry.
ex: I'll have to hustle to get there on time.
Men in dairy lunches were hustling to gulp down the food which cooks had hustled to fry

senses.d: To bundle; to stow something quickly.
To con, swindle, or deceive, especially financially.
ex: The guy tried to hustle me into buying into a bogus real estate deal.

senses.d: To play deliberately badly at a game or sport in an attempt to encourage players to challenge one.
To obtain by illicit or forceful action.
To sell sex; to work as a pimp.
To be a prostitute; to exchange use of one's body for sexual purposes for money.
ex: All my life, been hustling / And tonight is my appraisal / 'Cause I'm a hooker selling songs / And my pimp's a record label

senses.d: To serve (a clientele) as a prostitute.
ex: When I was in Morocco I wrote this play ("Playland Blues") about young kids who […] hustle old gay men and closet queens.

senses.d: To dance the hustle, a disco dance.
A state of busy activity.
A propensity to work hard and get things done; ability to hustle.
ex: 'It's just natural for the folks here to be indolent,' she said. 'They just haven't got any hustle in them.'

senses.d: A type of disco dance, commonly danced to the Van McCoy song The Hustle (1975).
A scam or swindle.
An activity, such as prostitution or reselling stolen items, that a prisoner uses to earn money in prison.
An act of prostitution.
ex: Little Joe never once gave it away / Everybody had to pay and pay / A hustle here and a hustle there / New York City's the place

senses.d: An activity, especially to achieve a desired goal or make money.
ex: Everybody's got a hustle.

fr:bousculer.gl: to shove, to bump into, to jostle

it:affrettarsi.gl: to hurry, hurry up, rush, hasten, race, make haste

it:darsi da fare.gl: to get busy, to get moving

es:darse prisa.gl: to hurry, to hurry up, to get a move on, to be quick, to make haste (to speed up the rate)

From cincha + -ar, or cincho + -ar.
Probably borrowed from Old French broueillier. Compare French embrouiller and Sicilian mprugghiari.

es:engañar.gl: to trick, to deceive, to hoodwink, to cheat

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. Compare Portuguese enganar, Catalan enganyar, Romanian îngâna, Italian ingannare. Cf. also Medieval Latin (in)gannatura (“mockery”).

es:engrupir.gl: to fool, deceive, trick, con, cheat, beguile (make someone believe a lie)

ety.text: From Lunfardo engrupo.
From bousculer + -ade.

fr:agitation.gl: choppiness (of water), turbulence (in air), swaying (of branch etc.)

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin agitātiōnem. By surface analysis, agiter + -ation.

1235; from Middle Breton cochuy (“covered market; bustle, tumult”) (modern Breton koc'hu, koc'hui), similar to Welsh cy- (“together”) + chwyf (“movement, commotion”), from Proto-Brythonic *hwɨβid (“to move”).
Deverbal from frettare + -a.

From the same Frankish/Germanic source as French tarabuster (“commotion, uproar”).
